The two sections after it do not depend on that answer. ### Summary Placeholder. Two or three sentences: basal α-richness is high, a loss term steers away from it, interface confidence pays for it, and Question 3 decides whether that payment is real. Write this after Question 3 resolves. ### A loss term is a tuning handle, and secondary structure is one thing to tune The steering result matters less for what it does to helices than for what it says about the method. A differentiable term added to the design loss changed the fold class of the output without retraining anything and without touching the model weights. The handle is the distogram the design loop already optimizes against, and it was sitting there unused. That reframes the contribution. This is not a paper about helices. It is a worked example of adding a constraint to ESMFold2's binder design algorithm, with the measurements needed to say honestly what the constraint bought and what it cost. The limits we ran into are part of the example, and they generalize: - The term stops acting once the property it penalizes is already saturated, so **when** a term applies during the run matters as much as how strongly. - Pushing harder on one property costs confidence in another, so any added term needs its tradeoff mapped rather than asserted. - The optimizer will satisfy a loss the cheapest way available, which is not always the way you intended. Anyone adding a term to this design loop should expect all three. ### A binder is the start of a drug program, not the end Nothing in this work produces a therapeutic. A design that binds its target with good predicted confidence has cleared the first of many gates. Downstream, a candidate still has to be developable: expressible and soluble at concentration, stable on the shelf, non-aggregating, humanized or otherwise non-immunogenic, free of manufacturing and post-translational liabilities, and specific enough not to bind everything else in the proteome. Each of those is a property of a sequence or a structure. That is the interesting part, because it is the same kind of object the secondary-structure term acts on. In principle every one of them is expressible as a term on the distogram or on the sequence logits, and added to the same objective in the same place. Sequence liabilities are the nearest example, and one worth tuning rather than ignoring. Steering the fold also changes the sequences that come out, so a term that optimizes structure alone can quietly degrade a property nobody was watching. We did not write a liability term here, and the designs in this work should not be read as developable. Adding one is the obvious next thing to try, and it would test whether the tuning handle generalizes beyond the property we happened to pick. That is the claim we want to leave the reader with: ESMFold2's binder design algorithm exposes a place to put constraints, secondary structure is one constraint that demonstrably works there, and the constraints a drug program actually cares about are the reason to care. ## Next steps Placeholder. What we would do next, and what someone else could pick up. Fill in once the takeaways are settled. ## An open question: objective or weights? Everything here changes behavior without changing the model. The steering happens in the design loop, on top of frozen weights, and that is worth naming as a choice rather than a default, because there is an obvious alternative: retrain or fine-tune so that the model produces the distribution you want natively. The two routes are not equivalent, and our results show some of the difference. Steering from the objective fights the model's prior instead of altering it, which may be why interface confidence pays a price, and why the optimizer sometimes satisfies the term in ways we did not intend. A model whose weights had learned the target distribution would presumably not need to be argued with in the same way. But the comparison is lopsided on cost. Adding a term to the loss is a few lines and a single campaign. Retraining a structure prediction model of this scale means substantial compute, a training corpus assembled for the property you want, and revalidation of everything the base model was already good at, with the risk of degrading it. For a property you might only want occasionally, or want in three mutually exclusive variants, that is a steep price. Post-hoc terms are also composable, inspectable, and trivially reversible, which weight updates are not. So we would pose it as a question rather than answer it. Which behaviors belong in the weights, and which belong in the objective? Is there a principled boundary, drawn perhaps by how fundamental a property is or how often it is wanted, or is the line mostly economic and therefore likely to move as training costs fall? We do not know, and the honest position from this work is that the objective route is cheap enough to be worth exhausting before anyone reaches for the weights.
